name: Aaron Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ruth and I bought Ridgeway Farm eleven years ago, with a mortgage that'll outlive the tractor. It's 110 hectares: 90 suckler cows raising beef calves, plus wheat and oats. The cows wear GPS collars, so I move them between paddocks from my phone, with no fences to shift. Every morning I check the herd on the app, then I'm out on the quad, then I pack beef boxes we sell online. An AI assistant writes most of my customer emails and helps me plan the grazing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Red tape. I can learn any machine in a week, but a new government form takes me a month to get right. Ruth runs a little bakery in town, and our kids are Daniel, fourteen, and Grace, eight. On Sundays I'm at church, where I'm an elder, and half the conversations after the service are about cattle prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? I'd be surprised, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are good and I'll keep using them, hype or no hype. The collars alone save me two days a week. I'd say that at the cattle society and probably post a video of the herd moving itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit let down. I was hoping for robots that could do the fencing and the heavy lifting. But it wouldn't hurt us, and the beef box business would keep growing on its own merits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and push the AI tools further, maybe planning the whole year's grazing and the beef box marketing. I'd look at adding a second batch of collars for the young stock, about 3,000. We'd keep saving our 200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little disappointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the other farmers at church make of the collars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half of them think I'm showing off, and the other half ask me quietly afterwards how much they cost. Old Mr Fenwick said he'd stick to his dog, and his dog is very good, to be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything else change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd still want to take on an apprentice next year, a local lad, because I believe in passing things on. That matters more to me than any gadget.

S0.say: The tools are good and I'll keep using them, hype or no hype. The GPS collars alone save me two days a week.
S0.think: I'd be a bit let down, because I was hoping for robots to do the fencing and heavy lifting. It wouldn't hurt us, and the beef box business would keep growing on its own merits.
S0.do: Keeps going and pushes AI further for grazing plans and beef box marketing. Considers a second batch of collars for young stock at about 3,000 and keeps saving 200 a month.
S0.quote: Old Mr Fenwick said he'd stick to his dog, and his dog is very good, to be fair.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is an early adopter with deeply traditional values: church, family and apprenticeships. He frames technology as a tool that rewards effort. His main frustration is government paperwork, not machines.

steps.text: Keep moving the 90 suckler cows by GPS collar and packing beef boxes
Get the AI to plan the whole year's grazing and the beef box marketing
Buy a second batch of collars for the young stock, about 3,000

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'm betting on, frankly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for farmers who are willing to work and learn. The market rewards people who adapt, and always has. I'd say that at the cattle society and to the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well, but I'd worry about the community. Some of the older farmers at church won't adapt, and they'll struggle. I'd want to help them rather than watch them sell up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd buy a fencing robot and a feed pusher, about 12,000, on a farm loan. I'd take on the apprentice and teach him the machines and the cattle both. And I'd offer to set up collars for two or three neighbours, for a fee, because they trust me more than a salesman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite energised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: 12,000 on a loan, with a mortgage already. Is Ruth on board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth would ask for the numbers, and she'd get them. She'd want to know what happens if beef prices drop, and we'd keep three months' savings untouched. She's more careful than me, and she's usually right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the government involved in helping those older farmers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather the community did it. Churches, the young farmers, people like me showing them how. Government help comes with forms, and forms are what put the older farmers off in the first place.

S1.say: This is good news for farmers who are willing to work and learn. The market rewards people who adapt, and always has.
S1.think: I'd do well, but I'd worry about the older farmers at church who won't adapt and will struggle. I'd want to help them rather than watch them sell up.
S1.do: Buys a fencing robot and feed pusher for about 12,000 on a farm loan, keeping three months' savings untouched. Takes on an apprentice and charges neighbours to set up GPS collars for them.
S1.quote: Government help comes with forms, and forms are what put the older farmers off in the first place.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron would move fast on automation and turn his know-how into a side income. His concern is community, specifically older farmers at church. He prefers community help over government help and blames paperwork.

steps.text: Bring a fencing robot and a feed pusher onto Ridgeway Farm
Borrow about 12,000 for the machines, keeping three months' savings untouched
Set up GPS collars for two or three neighbours, for a fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the forms go first and the fencing later. I could live with that order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the cattle society I'd say it's the best news farmers have had in years: the paperwork goes in 2028 and we've got three years to get ready for the robots. I'd tell the young farmers to learn the machines now and not wait. I'd say it with a straight face, because I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased and a bit nervous at the same time. The AI doing my forms and planning the grazing is a gift, I've wanted that for years. The worry is 2031, when the big beef outfits get robots too and the price per kilo drops, and I don't want to be holding a big loan when that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd hand every form, the grazing plan and the beef box marketing to the AI, and get two days a week back. I'd use those days to pay the 12,000 machinery loan off by 2030, not 2033, so we're clear before the price falls. I'd buy only machines that pay for themselves in a season. And I'd sell the robot know-how to neighbours, setting up their systems for a fee, while I'm the one who knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly excited. Like starting a long drive with a good map and one tyre I'm not sure about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Daniel? He'd be seventeen by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that sits in my chest. Daniel likes the cattle, but I don't know what a young stockman does when a robot can do the stock work. I'd want my son to learn the machines and the animals, so he's the one fixing them, not watching them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the older farmers at church would struggle. What happens to them here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years isn't long for a man of seventy who still uses a paper diary. I'd go round after the service with my laptop and set up the AI for their forms myself, for nothing. If I can save Mr Fenwick a month of paperwork, that's worth more than any fee.

S2.say: It's the best news farmers have had in years: the paperwork goes in 2028 and we've got three years to get ready for the robots. Young farmers should learn the machines now and not wait.
S2.think: The AI doing my forms and grazing plans is a gift I've wanted for years. The worry is 2031, when the big beef outfits get robots, the price per kilo drops, and I don't want to be holding a big loan.
S2.do: Hands every form, the grazing plan and the beef box marketing to the AI in 2028, freeing two days a week. Pays the 12,000 machinery loan off by 2030 instead of 2033, and sets up robot systems for neighbours for a fee.
S2.feel: Uneasy but mostly excited, like starting a long drive with a good map and one doubtful tyre.
S2.quote: If I can save Mr Fenwick a month of paperwork, that's worth more than any fee.
S2.fieldNote: Aaron welcomes the thinking AI because it takes the red tape he hates, and treats the three years before robots as a deadline to clear his debt. His worry is the beef price from 2031 and his son's future, not his own skills. He'd spend part of his freed time helping older church farmers for free.

steps.text: Hand Ridgeway's forms, grazing plan and beef box marketing to the AI
Pay off the 12,000 machinery loan by 2030 instead of 2033
Set up robot and collar systems for neighbouring farms for a fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then eight for the robots. That's my kind of timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this rewards farmers who get on with it. Five years is enough to learn it all and be ready. I'd say that at the cattle society and to the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well. I'd have the AI running the paperwork from 2031 and robots on the farm before 2034. With two years of warning I'm caught holding debt, but with five I'm the man selling the know-how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd buy the fencing robot and feed pusher and take on an apprentice, a local lad. By year two I'd build a side business setting up robots and collars for other farms. I'd bring Daniel in during the school holidays to learn alongside the apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and energised, like spring when the grass starts moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the community lose, even if you did well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older farmers would sell up, and the church would feel it. Machines can do the work, but they can't raise a family or run a community. That's still our job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth's bakery do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's bread is hands-on, so she'd have till 2034 like me. I think people would still pay for a loaf made by someone they know. She'd use the AI for her orders, and she'd tell me to stop going on about it.

S3.say: This rewards farmers who get on with it. Five years is enough to learn it all and be ready.
S3.think: I'd do well, with the AI running paperwork from 2031 and robots on the farm before 2034. With two years of warning I'm caught holding debt, but with five I'm the man selling the know-how.
S3.do: Buys the fencing robot and feed pusher and takes on a local apprentice in year one. Builds a side business setting up robots and collars for other farms by year two, and brings Daniel in during school holidays.
S3.feel: Calm and energised, like spring when the grass starts moving.
S3.quote: With two years of warning I'm caught holding debt, but with five I'm the man selling the know-how.
S3.fieldNote: With eight years before robots, Aaron sees a clear business opening in teaching neighbours the machines. His traditional values show in his worry for the church community and his plan to train an apprentice and his son together. He also thinks his wife's bakery has time on its side.

steps.text: Buy the fencing robot and feed pusher and take on a local apprentice
Start a side business setting up robots and collars for other farms
Bring Daniel onto the farm in school holidays to learn the machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten and thirteen years. Plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out, and that the market will reward the people who prepare. I'd tell the young farmers to learn steadily. A decade is a gift if you use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd love it. I'd automate step by step so the debt never runs ahead of the money. By 2039 I'd be 56, with Daniel grown and perhaps farming with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with one robot in year one and add more only as each one proves itself. I'd take on an apprentice every two years. And I'd save 50 a month each for Daniel and Grace's apprenticeships or college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Daniel learn from the robots or from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. Either way, I'd want my son to know how to calve a cow by hand, even if a machine usually does it. There's always a night when the machine breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You asked what robots leave us to do. What's your own answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching, I think. Passing it on. If the robots do the lifting, I'd spend more time with apprentices and with the old men at church, and less time on the quad.

S4.say: There's no excuse for anyone to be caught out, and the market will reward the people who prepare. A decade is a gift if you use it.
S4.think: I'd love it, automating step by step so the debt never runs ahead of the money. By 2039 I'd be 56, with Daniel grown and perhaps farming with me.
S4.do: Starts with one robot in year one and adds more only as each proves itself. Takes on an apprentice every two years and saves 50 a month each for Daniel and Grace's apprenticeships or college.
S4.quote: I'd want my son to know how to calve a cow by hand, even if a machine usually does it.
S4.fieldNote: With a long timeline Aaron is fully at ease and focused on passing skills on. He answers his own question about what robots leave people to do: teaching and community. He insists his son should keep the old hands-on skills for the night the machine breaks.

steps.text: Start with one robot in year one and add more only as each pays back
Save 50 a month each for Daniel and Grace's apprenticeships or college

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would come in 2031 and beef prices would fall while I'm still holding loans, and three years is short to pay them down. What would help is less red tape so farmers can move quickly, and the banks giving family farms a bit of breathing room on loans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about dignity. Everyone talks about jobs and money. But a man who doesn't work loses something, and I'd want to know what the robots leave us to do.

headlineQuote: Machines can do the work, but they can't raise a family or run a community.
portrait: Aaron Okafor, 43, and his wife bought Ridgeway Farm eleven years ago and run 90 suckler cows with wheat and oats, selling beef boxes online. He uses AI and GPS cattle collars every day, and combines early adoption with traditional values: church, family, apprenticeships and little patience for red tape. He stays calm through AI stalling and steady change, and sees a side business in setting up robots for neighbours. Fast AGI only makes him uneasy: he'd welcome the AI taking his paperwork in 2028 and race to pay off his machinery loan before robots push beef prices down in 2031. With more time he plans step-by-step automation, training young people and his son.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because robots would push beef prices down from 2031 while he's still holding loans, with little time to pay them down.
whatWouldHelp: Less red tape so farmers can move quickly, and banks giving family farms breathing room on loans.
